label: Naming Conventions
language: TypeScript

repository_stars: 70984
---

Names for variables, parameters, fields, and functions should describe the actual domain concept they represent, not an implementation detail, and should read naturally without requiring the reader to negate or decode them.

- Avoid vague booleans whose meaning only becomes clear through negation (e.g. `background` used as `!background`). Name the condition directly from the perspective that matters to callers, e.g. `userInitiated`, so checks read as `if (userInitiated)`.
- When a field can take more than two meaningfully different states, or when "false" doesn't describe a real, nameable state, prefer a string literal union/enum over a boolean. For example, instead of `entry?: boolean` with an implicit "not set" meaning, use `entry?: "run" | "continue"` so every state is named positively instead of inferred from absence.
- When exporting multiple functions that solve closely related problems (e.g. `findUsableFallbackProviderId` vs `resolveEffectiveLastUsedProviderId`), make sure their names alone signal which one callers should use. If both must remain public, give them maximally distinct, intention-revealing names and document precisely when to use each; otherwise, collapse them into a single public entry point and keep the helper internal (e.g. exported only for tests via a clearly-marked internal namespace).

The guiding question before naming anything is: "If someone unfamiliar with this code only sees the name, will they understand what it represents and pick the right one without reading the implementation?" If not, rename it.
